830: More than 25% above hurts your reputation. Much cheaper improves it a little, but you give up margin.
831: If it's 2, raising the price 1% lowers demand by about 2%.
832: Base cost × quality × inflation. Volume discount: %s%s
835: Price − variable cost. What each sale contributes to pay fixed costs.
837: Capacity = employees × productivity. If demand exceeds it, you lose sales.
839: Percentage of demand you managed to serve. If it's low, your reputation drops.
842: Daily fixed costs of the line (%s) ÷ contribution margin.
848: Open a branch to see the curve.
851: Inferior good: sells MORE in a recession, but higher risk of fines.
853: Customers less sensitive to price, but it drops hard in a recession.
856: Diminishing returns: brand awareness rises with the budget, but each extra dollar does less. If you stop investing, people slowly forget you.
859: Depends on quality, serving all demand and not charging much more than the market.
861: Every morning you buy what's needed to cover N days of sales. Little inventory = you run out if demand rises. Lots = more waste and storage cost.
866: Inventory lost each day (it spoils or becomes obsolete).
867: The manager handles this line's inventory.
870: Economies of scale: the supplier gives you a better price if you bought more from them last month.
873: More competitors = fewer customers for you. They arrive when the market leaves a big margin.
876: Leverage: a loan lets you invest sooner, but you pay interest even if you sell little. More debt relative to equity = higher rate.
879: Central bank rate + 3% + risk premium based on your debt/equity.
881: Depends on your fixed assets, your inventory and your recent EBITDA.
889: Equal payments. At first you pay more interest; at the end, more principal.
896: You pay %s today (the balance plus interest for the days so far this month) and save the future interest.
898: Risk-free investment that pays the central bank rate. It's the opportunity cost of your money: any investment in the business should earn more than this.
905: Opportunity cost: if a branch earns less than these bonds, that money would be better off here. If it earns more, invest it in the business.
908: Paid every month on pre-tax profit. Interest and depreciation reduce the base (tax shield).
910: Losses from previous months are deducted from future profits before paying taxes.
913: If your cash stays below this limit for 20 days in a row, the bank declares you bankrupt.
916: Diseconomies of scale: coordinating many branches costs more and more. Investing in systems lowers that cost and lets you keep growing.
921: They grow faster than the number of branches (from the sixth on).
922: You have the best management system. Your corporate overhead is 88% lower than when you started.
925: With more branches the savings grow. The investment depreciates over 5 years like any asset.
930: Risk and return: on average it earns more than bonds, but it goes up and down every day and falls hard in a recession.
933: It changes with the economic cycle. Bonds earn the central bank rate.
941: In normal mode the game ends at Empire. To keep going for more titles, start a game in investor mode.
942: To keep growing: management systems so corporate overhead doesn't eat your profit, and your cash working in the fund or in bonds.
966: What the operation generates before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
968: Investment in branches, factories and licenses spread over 5 years. It's not a cash outflow.
969: Diseconomies of scale: headquarters grows faster than the number of branches (from the 6th on).
970: Product that spoiled, became obsolete or was lost.
971: What you actually earned. This is the bottom line.
973: Snapshot of the company today: what you have (assets) = what you owe (liabilities) + what's yours (equity).
